stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Great Society changed the role of the federal government in American life from 1964 to 1968.

documents.title: An unconditional war on poverty
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson, State of the Union address, January 8, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Johnson is speaking to Congress as president, asking it to fund a new program, so he frames poverty as a war the nation must win.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson, State of the Union address, January 8, 1964. Johnson declared an unconditional war on poverty in America. He said the nation would not rest until the war was won, and he asked Congress to pass laws that would give poor Americans education, training, and work.

documents.title: The Great Society
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, May 22, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Johnson is speaking to graduating students, so he sets out a broad vision of American life rather than the details of any one bill.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, May 22, 1964. Johnson said, "The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time." He named three places to begin building it: "in our cities, in our countryside, and in our classrooms."

documents.title: Opportunity, not charity
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964, Public Law 88-452, signed August 20, 1964.
documents.sourcing: The act is a law, so its stated purpose shows what Congress meant the program to do, not only what Johnson hoped for.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964, signed August 20, 1964. The act said it was the policy of the United States "to eliminate the paradox of poverty in the midst of plenty" by opening to everyone "the opportunity for education and training, the opportunity to work, and the opportunity to live in decency and dignity." It created the Office of Economic Opportunity to run the Job Corps, VISTA, and community action programs.

documents.title: Extremism in the defense of liberty
documents.source: Paraphrase of Senator Barry Goldwater, acceptance speech, Republican National Convention, July 16, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Goldwater is accepting his party's nomination, so he states his opposition in the strongest terms to rally his supporters.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Senator Barry Goldwater, acceptance speech, July 16, 1964. Goldwater said, "Extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice." He argued that the federal government had grown too large and that its welfare programs threatened freedom, so the growth of government itself had to be rolled back.

documents.title: Medicare becomes law
documents.source: Paraphrase of the signing of the Social Security Amendments of 1965, July 30, 1965, in Independence, Missouri.
documents.sourcing: The signing ceremony honored former President Truman as the first Medicare beneficiary, so it links the new law to Truman's 1945 proposal for national health insurance.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the signing of the Social Security Amendments of 1965, July 30, 1965. President Lyndon Johnson signed the law creating Medicare, health insurance for Americans 65 and older, and Medicaid, medical coverage for Americans who could not afford their own insurance. Former President Harry S. Truman, then 81 years old, received the first Medicare card.

documents.title: A new door for immigrants
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, Public Law 89-236, signed October 3, 1965.
documents.sourcing: The act is a law, so its limits and exemptions show how Congress changed immigration, not only what its supporters hoped for.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, signed October 3, 1965. The act abolished the national quota system based on national origins that had been in place since the 1920s. It set overall limits instead: 170,000 immigrants a year from the Eastern Hemisphere and 120,000 a year from the Western Hemisphere. In the years that followed, migration from Asia, Africa, and Latin America rose sharply.

documents.title: Poverty falls, but does not end
documents.source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, Historical Poverty Tables, Table 2.
documents.sourcing: The Census Bureau counts poverty by income, so the table measures how many Americans were poor, not whether government programs caused the change.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Great Society changed the role of the federal government in American life from 1964 to 1968, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of the change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as postwar prosperity and the persistence of poverty, the New Deal's expansion of the federal role, or the civil rights movement of the early 1960s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant examples of the Great Society changing the federal role, such as the Office of Economic Opportunity, Medicare and Medicaid, or federal aid to schools.
rubric.notEarned: Naming programs without describing what they did does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (second point): earns the point for supporting the argument with evidence from at least six documents, using the documents to show both change and its limits.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (third point): earns the point for using at least one piece of specific outside evidence, such as Head Start, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, or the Higher Education Act.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating only what the documents say, with no outside evidence, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the sourcing of a document shapes its meaning, such as Goldwater speaking to rally his party's supporters, or the Census table measuring income poverty rather than the cause of the fall.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author or date without explaining how it shapes the document does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing the change was deep and partial at once, such as the federal role growing in health, education, and housing while poverty did not end and critics pushed back against the growth of government.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that the change was total or that nothing changed does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Great Society changed the role of the federal government to a great extent from 1964 to 1968, putting Washington into health care, education, housing, and the fight against poverty, though the change was partial, since poverty did not end and the growth of government drew strong opposition.
Context: The United States came out of World War II prosperous, yet millions stayed poor; the New Deal had already shown that Washington could act, and the civil rights movement was pressing the government to do more.
Evidence: Document 1 declares an unconditional war on poverty. Document 2 sets the vision of abundance and liberty for all. Document 3 creates the Office of Economic Opportunity and its programs. Document 5 creates Medicare and Medicaid. Document 6 ends the national-origins quotas. Document 7 shows the poverty rate falling from 19.0 percent in 1964 to 14.7 percent in 1966.
Outside evidence: Head Start prepared disadvantaged preschool children for school, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act sent federal grants to poor schools, and the Department of Housing and Urban Development supervised affordable housing.
Complexity: Document 4 shows Goldwater arguing the growth of government threatened freedom, and Document 7 shows 14.7 percent of Americans still poor in 1966, so the federal role grew greatly without finishing the job.
